table.brief: i18n string table: Key (like checkout.button.confirm) / English / 中文 / 日本語 / العربية — five columns of short UI strings

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: d2r2A
candidates.idea: Refine the strongest scrolling layout with more room for English and Chinese while retaining whole keys and the effective Japanese and Arabic widths.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: 有効なメールアドレスを

whys: Unbroken keys and short, mostly natural lines make the full table clear and compact. The first viewport cuts through English, and reaching the other languages requires substantial horizontal scrolling.
Whole keys and mostly short rows support lookup, with no measured internal word breaks. The initial viewport cuts through English text, and the Chinese shipping entry leaves a lone final character.

Whole keys and words, short cells and clear row alignment make the full table easy to read. The initial viewport cuts into English, however, and reaching translations requires substantial horizontal scrolling.

candidates.name: d2r1B
candidates.idea: Test a fitting alternative that redistributes space from the key to all four translations. This will split keys more aggressively, but may improve header and phrase readability while keeping every language visible at once; the trade-off needs a render.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The wider key column reduces fragmentation and row height compared with A and B. Keys, English words and some translations still split awkwardly, and the English header wraps.
The wider key column improves scanning over A and G, but identifiers and English words still break internally, and narrow translation columns produce crowded, uneven rows.

Wider keys reduce some fragmentation and row height compared with A, while all columns remain visible. Identifiers, English words and Arabic still break awkwardly, and the narrow Chinese and Japanese columns make longer strings hard to follow.

candidates.name: d1r4B
candidates.idea: Refine d1r1B by giving Chinese and Arabic more room, aiming to remove the remaining internal word break and improve phrase wrapping while keeping the complete key and English columns in the initial viewport.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: 有効なメールアドレス

whys: Keys and English are fully visible initially, and the full table has no measured word breaks. Most translations fit on one or two lines, though the last Chinese line is a single character and the far columns require considerable scrolling.

Keys remain intact, English is fully visible initially, and translations generally wrap into readable units. The Chinese shipping entry ends with a lone character, and comparing translations requires scrolling.

Whole keys and words and mostly short, well-spaced translations support clear reading. The initial viewport shows keys and English together, although comparing them with translations still requires considerable scrolling; the Chinese shipping string ends with a lone character.

candidates.name: d3r1A
candidates.idea: Refine the scrolling design: preserve whole keys, give English and Arabic more room for word boundaries, and give Japanese and Chinese more room for the longest translations. Test whether the additional width improves the tall error row without approaching C's scrolling distance.
candidates.label: gold

lineInfo.text: 有効なメールアドレス

whys: Complete keys and English fit in the first viewport; the full table has short lines and a steadier rhythm than E. One measured word break remains, and the translated columns require scrolling.
Whole keys, concise rows and mostly natural translation wraps make this a balanced scrolling layout. One measured internal break remains, and the translated columns start beyond the initial viewport.

Whole keys and mostly natural two-line translations give the table a compact, orderly structure. The key and English columns fit at first sight, though one measured word break and scrolling to translations limit it.
The first viewport shows complete keys and English, and the full table is relatively compact. The narrow Chinese and Japanese columns create awkward breaks and a conspicuously tall error row.
Whole keys and a compact grid make lookup straightforward. Some Chinese and Japanese lines break awkwardly, including an isolated final character, and translations require scrolling into view.

The initial view shows complete keys and English, and the table needs less horizontal travel than the other viable scrolling layouts. Narrower translation columns produce more awkward wraps, including a lone Chinese character and a three-line Japanese cell.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Equal widths appear orderly but give the long identifiers far too little room. They would also force English and Arabic words to break while allocating width without regard to each script's content.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The grid remains intact, but identifiers and English words break repeatedly, including the English header. Tall, uneven rows make scanning and comparing translations difficult.
All columns are visible, but keys fragment across several lines, English splits inside words, and the long Japanese entry creates a conspicuously tall row.
All columns are visible at once, but keys, English words and the English header break arbitrarily. Tall rows and narrow fragments make scanning and comparison laborious.
Whole keys are gained at the cost of almost single-character Chinese and Japanese columns. Wrapped headers and a 19-line cell create enormous rows, while scrolling is still needed.
Keys stay whole, but Chinese and Japanese are forced into nearly single-character lines. The very tall rows make comparison difficult, despite requiring horizontal scrolling.

Intact keys come at the cost of Chinese and Japanese squeezed into near single-character lines, split headers and extremely tall rows. The table still requires scrolling, making lookup and comparison particularly difficult.
Like A, the narrow columns fragment keys and words and produce very tall rows. The slight width difference does not materially improve reading or lookup.
Like A, it shows all five columns at once but fragments keys and English words heavily. The long Japanese cell drives a tall row and interrupts the table's rhythm.
The full grid fits, but keys, English words and the English header are split into fragments. Its tall, uneven rows make the strings difficult to scan; the result is visually almost identical to A.

d1.purpose: Present checkout interface strings by key so readers can find a message and compare its translations.
tasks: Find a string by its key or English wording.
Read across a row to check the corresponding translations.
Scan a language column to review wording and consistency.
relations: Each row joins one stable key to four versions of the same message.
The English text provides source context for interpreting the translations.
The shipping estimate contains the same 3–5 day range across languages.
roles: The first column identifies each string and acts as the row header.
The four language columns contain parallel message text.
The top row labels the key and each language.
keep_whole: Keys should remain intact whenever space permits; their punctuation is meaningful.
Words, email-related terminology and the 3–5 range should stay together where possible.
Arabic text should retain natural word boundaries and right-to-left reading order.
may_wrap: English and Arabic phrases may wrap at word boundaries.
Chinese and Japanese sentences may wrap at natural character or phrase boundaries.
same_scale: The four language columns have parallel roles, but their widths may differ to accommodate their writing systems and message lengths.
The key column merits extra space because its identifiers contain long unbreakable units.
d1.h_vs_v: A phone-width table forces long keys and some words to split, increasing row heights and making comparison harder. Scrolling preserves readable units but places some languages beyond the initial viewport; a wider table reduces wrapping at the cost of more horizontal travel.

d2.purpose: Present checkout interface strings by key and language so readers can find and compare translations.
tasks: Find a string by its key.
Read the corresponding text in one or more languages.
Compare translations across a row and check wording.
relations: Each row links one identifier to equivalent interface text in four languages.
The key identifies the string; the language columns contain peer translations.
roles: The first column contains row headers used for lookup.
The remaining columns are language-specific text, with headers identifying each language.
Each body row represents one interface message.
keep_whole: Keys and their dot-separated identifiers where space permits.
Words, email-related terms and the 3–5 range where possible.
may_wrap: English and Arabic phrases at natural word boundaries.
Chinese and Japanese text at natural script-appropriate break points.
same_scale: The four translation columns should have broadly comparable visual weight, adjusted for their scripts and content lengths.
All keys share the same lookup role.
d2.h_vs_v: A fitting table exposes all languages at once but forces severe wrapping, including within long keys. Scrolling preserves identifiers and gives translations room to read; wider columns reduce row height at the cost of more horizontal travel.

d3.purpose: Provide a multilingual reference for checkout interface strings keyed by their implementation identifiers.
tasks: Find a string by key and read its translations.
Compare the wording and meaning across languages in the same row.
Check individual translations for completeness and consistency.
relations: Each row joins one implementation key to equivalent English, Chinese, Japanese and Arabic strings.
The English column provides a readily readable reference for interpreting the other translations.
The six keys describe distinct interface messages rather than visible row groups.
roles: The header row identifies the key and each language.
The first column contains row headers used for lookup.
The four language columns contain interface labels and short messages.
keep_whole: Implementation keys should remain intact wherever space permits.
Words, email-related terminology and the 3–5 range should remain intact.
Arabic words should remain whole and retain their natural right-to-left reading order.
may_wrap: English and Arabic phrases may wrap between words.
Chinese and Japanese sentences may wrap at natural script-appropriate boundaries, avoiding awkward breaks within closely related terms where possible.
same_scale: Language columns share the same structural role, but their widths should reflect differences in script and string length.
Row labels should have a consistent width that supports scanning the identifiers.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport fit exposes all languages at once but forces severe wrapping and splits identifiers. Scrolling can preserve keys and improve reading, at the cost of hiding some languages on first sight; a wider table reduces row height but makes cross-language comparison require more horizontal movement.

analysis.strengths: English and Arabic have somewhat more room than in several other fitting layouts, and all five columns are visible at once.
analysis.faults: The Chinese column forces near-vertical reading, Japanese is heavily fragmented, and two headers wrap. Keys break repeatedly, and the long error row becomes exceptionally tall.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space is spread relatively evenly among the Latin and Arabic columns, leaving Chinese especially narrow. The resulting tall CJK cells determine the rhythm of the whole table.

analysis.strengths: It is the most compact fitting layout shown and keeps the Chinese, Japanese and Arabic headers on one line. Its wider key column reduces some identifier fragmentation.
analysis.faults: English words and its header split, keys remain difficult to scan, and Arabic words also break. The error row is still very tall and difficult to read across.
analysis.spatial_logic: It favors the key and Japanese columns within the fixed viewport, accepting narrow English and Arabic columns. This reduces height compared with P and T but trades away word integrity.

analysis.strengths: Whole keys and words remain intact, the headers are clear, and most rows are short. The generous language columns make comparison comfortable in the full view.
analysis.faults: It requires the most horizontal scrolling. At first sight, the key consumes most of the viewport and the English column is cut off; a few Chinese and Arabic phrases wrap awkwardly despite the overall width.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives each column enough room for relatively open text setting, prioritizing short rows and unbroken units over the amount of table visible on a phone.

analysis.strengths: The full key and English columns fit at first sight, making the initial view useful for lookup. It is the narrowest scrolling layout shown, and its language columns remain substantially more readable than those in the fitting layouts.
analysis.faults: One measured word break remains, and the narrow Chinese column produces less natural wrapping in longer entries. Several rows are taller than in R, while the other languages still require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: It uses the exact key-plus-English viewport as a strong first screen, then compresses the remaining columns to reduce the scrolling distance.

analysis.strengths: Its wider key column gives identifiers more room, and all columns are initially visible. English is less constrained than in Q.
analysis.faults: Japanese and Arabic headers wrap, Arabic words split, and Japanese becomes a narrow vertical strip. The long error row is much taller than in Q, while keys still break inside identifiers.
analysis.spatial_logic: It concentrates scarce width on the key and English, taking it from Japanese and Arabic. The gains in the first two columns do not compensate for the severe fragmentation elsewhere.

analysis.strengths: Whole keys and measured words remain intact, and the full key and English columns fit at first sight. The wider Arabic column improves its longer entries compared with S.
analysis.faults: It requires substantial scrolling, and the Chinese shipping entry leaves a single character on its second line. English wraps several short phrases, making more rows tall than in R.
analysis.spatial_logic: It preserves S's useful first viewport while spending additional width on Chinese and Arabic to improve language readability.

rounds.insights: The long unbreakable keys make a fully readable five-column table impossible at phone width under the fixed styling. Among fitting layouts, Q is the strongest compromise, though its broken words and identifiers remain serious faults. Scrolling protects content integrity; S and U make especially good use of the first viewport by showing complete key and English columns, while R buys shorter rows at the cost of a partially visible English column. The best allocation depends on actual phrase breaks, not equal column widths or total height alone.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are available without scrolling, and English remains comparatively readable.
analysis.faults: Identifiers and Arabic words break repeatedly; the Japanese and Arabic headers wrap, and the Japanese error message forms a very tall, narrow stack.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow language columns turn the error row into a large vertical interruption and leave neighboring cells disproportionately empty.

analysis.strengths: Complete keys and English are visible together on first sight. Most translations are readable in one or two lines.
analysis.faults: One measured word break remains, and several English phrases wrap. The other languages require substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A generous Chinese column keeps its shipping string on one line but adds width without reducing the height set by English.

analysis.strengths: It retains the useful initial key-and-English view while reducing scrolling compared with s0B.
analysis.faults: One measured word break remains. Chinese shipping wraps, as do several English strings, and the language columns remain off-screen initially.
analysis.spatial_logic: Narrowing Chinese saves width at no height cost because English already makes the shipping row two lines.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once, and the additional Japanese width reduces the extreme height seen in s0A.
analysis.faults: The English header, English words, identifiers and Arabic words split unnaturally. The dense error row remains difficult to read.
analysis.spatial_logic: Width moved toward Japanese improves the tallest row, but the resulting narrow English column spreads awkward breaks across the table.

analysis.strengths: All identifiers and words remain intact, and more rows fit on one line than in the other scrolling layouts. The compact height supports scanning.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through English content, so some phrases require scrolling even before reaching the translations. Chinese and Arabic shipping strings wrap, and the total scroll distance is substantial.
analysis.spatial_logic: Extra English width shortens several rows, producing a compact table, but places the viewport boundary inside the English column.

analysis.strengths: There are no measured breaks inside words, and complete keys and English are visible together initially. The table is narrower than R.
analysis.faults: Several English phrases wrap, Chinese shipping ends with a lone character, and all translations require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The width allocation favors the initial lookup view, but its narrow English column determines several row heights while other cells have spare vertical space.

rounds.insights: At phone width, the unbreakable identifiers compete directly with the space needed for four languages. Fitting every column makes the table available at once but severely damages continuous reading. Scrolling preserves words and keys; within that class, a complete initial key-and-English view competes with the shorter rows obtained by widening English. Chinese width can often be reduced without increasing overall row height, but a lone final character is an undesirable break.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are visible at once, and the English header and most English words remain intact.
analysis.faults: Identifiers break repeatedly, three headers wrap, and the Chinese column becomes nearly vertical. The validation row is exceptionally tall, making both lookup and comparison arduous.
analysis.spatial_logic: More width goes to English than in Q, but the narrow Chinese and Japanese columns produce extreme row heights and uneven density.

analysis.strengths: Complete identifiers and single-line headers establish a clear hierarchy. Most rows are compact, and translations are generally easy to read.
analysis.faults: One measured word break remains. The initial viewport cuts into English, and the reader must scroll a long way to reach Arabic.
analysis.spatial_logic: The wide key column protects lookup labels, while generous language columns keep the table short; the cost is a large horizontal span.

analysis.strengths: All languages can be compared without scrolling. Compared with s1A, more width for Chinese and Japanese substantially reduces height, and four headers stay on one line.
analysis.faults: The English header and many English words split, identifiers remain fragmented, and Arabic words also break. The long validation row still disrupts scanning.
analysis.spatial_logic: The redistribution improves the vertical rhythm of the fitted table, but the narrow English column makes ordinary phrases difficult to read.

analysis.strengths: Identifiers and headers stay whole, no word breaks are measured, and most rows are single-line. It is narrower than s1C while retaining the same compact height.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts off part of English; Chinese and Arabic shipping translations each leave a short final line. Reaching later languages requires substantial scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A protected key column and a comparatively wide Japanese column support lookup and compact rows. Some space saved in Chinese and Arabic creates less natural endings.

analysis.strengths: Identifiers and headers stay whole, no word breaks are measured, and the first viewport contains the complete key and English columns. It is the narrowest scrolling candidate.
analysis.faults: Several English phrases wrap, increasing row heights, and the Chinese shipping translation leaves a single character on its second line. Later languages still require substantial scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: Reducing English to fit alongside the key in the initial viewport improves first-sight utility, at the expense of a taller table and more uneven row rhythm.

rounds.insights: The fitted layouts expose every language at once but cannot preserve long identifiers and words within 360 px. Q is the stronger fitted example, though its English breaks are costly. Scrolling allows intact identifiers and much more natural text; R favors compact rows, while U makes the full key–English pair available immediately. The Chinese shipping line in R and U suggests that a small width increase could improve line endings without changing the overall strategy.

analysis.strengths: All five columns are visible without scrolling, and most English headings and short strings remain recognizable.
analysis.faults: Identifiers, Arabic words and some English words break internally. Japanese and Arabic headings wrap, and the long Japanese error message becomes a nine-line column of fragments.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow language columns create a very tall error row and uneven density; the modest width given to the key still cannot preserve identifiers.

analysis.strengths: Whole identifiers, single-line headings and mostly short rows make the full table easy to scan. The Chinese shipping string stays on one line.
analysis.faults: One measured break falls inside a word. At the initial scroll position the viewport cuts through English values, while the other languages are offscreen.
analysis.spatial_logic: Generous language widths keep the table compact vertically, but its 893px width requires substantial horizontal travel.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once. Compared with s2A, a little more room for Japanese and Arabic reduces the tallest row and overall height.
analysis.faults: The English header and many English words split internally, as do identifiers and Arabic words. The long error row remains difficult to read across.
analysis.spatial_logic: Shifting width from English to Japanese and Arabic improves vertical rhythm but transfers fragmentation to English. It is the stronger fitting candidate by height and break count, though still severely compromised.

analysis.strengths: Identifiers and words remain whole, headings are single-line, and only two rows need two lines. The Japanese error message has a more comfortable measure than in the narrower candidates.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through English values and hides all three translation columns. The Chinese shipping string leaves a single final character on the second line.
analysis.spatial_logic: A wide key and generous English and Japanese columns support quick scanning in the full table, at the cost of 523px of horizontal overflow.

analysis.strengths: The initial viewport shows the full key and English columns, with whole words and identifiers. Its narrower overall width reduces horizontal travel, and the Arabic shipping string fits on one line.
analysis.faults: English wraps in several rows, making the table taller. The Chinese shipping string ends with a single character on a second line, and translations still require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first two columns are tuned to the phone viewport, giving a coherent initial view; the narrower English column trades vertical compactness for that useful first sight.

rounds.insights: The fitting layouts expose every language at once but fragment identifiers and words so heavily that lookup and continuous reading suffer. Scrolling preserves the content, but the initial viewport matters: R is compact in the full view while U presents complete key–English pairs at first sight. A little more Chinese width may avoid the isolated final character, and a modest English increase may recover some of R's compactness while keeping most of U's first-view benefit.

bad.why: The narrow key and Japanese columns fragment identifiers and text; the longest Japanese cell reaches nine lines, and the Japanese header wraps.
Identifiers break repeatedly, Chinese is reduced almost to one character per line, and the Arabic shipping range is broken across lines. The result is unusually tall and difficult to scan.
Keys and Arabic words break within their units, two headers wrap, and the narrow Japanese column produces a ten-line cell.

contrast.why: Equal widths appear orderly but give the long identifiers far too little room. They would also force English and Arabic words to break while allocating width without regard to each script's content.

sameFunctionGroups.why: All four columns contain translations of the same strings, so they deserve comparable visual prominence. Their scripts and line lengths differ, however, so equal widths would not give them equally readable measures.

synthesis.rationale: R preserves complete keys and words, keeps all headers on one line, and limits cells to two lines; its main cost is substantial horizontal scrolling. Q is the strongest fitting candidate, with fewer measured word breaks and less height than the other fitting layouts, but it still fragments keys, English and Arabic and is a qualified finalist only because a fitting option is required. U offers a useful scrolling alternative: the key and English columns fit at first sight, though several English entries wrap and the full table is taller.

general: Protect identifiers, words and meaningful number ranges when assigning column widths.
Judge a scrolling table both as a whole and at its initial viewport.
Give columns with the same function consistent prominence, while sizing them for their actual content and writing systems.
specific: The key column needs 227 px to accommodate its longest identifier with the stated padding and border.
At this viewport width, fitting all five columns entails severe fragmentation; Q is the least compromised of the rendered fitting candidates.

synthesis.tradeoffs: R favors readable strings and compact rows but requires 523 px of horizontal travel and initially shows only part of English. U uses 28 px less total width and shows the full English column initially, at the cost of more wrapped rows. Q shows all languages at once but makes lookup and continuous reading substantially harder.
synthesis.uncertain: The measured single word break in s2C, s3B and S is not identified by cell, so its practical severity is uncertain. Acceptance of Q depends on whether avoiding horizontal scrolling is valuable enough to justify its substantial reading faults; it would not be my preferred production choice.

critique.good: All five columns are visible together, so the language headings and row relationships remain in view without scrolling.
critique.problems: Keys and English words break across lines, two headings wrap, and the Japanese and Arabic text becomes difficult to read in narrow fragments. The unusually tall email row disrupts scanning and makes corresponding translations hard to compare.
critique.cause: The 105px key column cannot hold the identifiers; the 70px English and 64px Arabic columns split words. The 55px Chinese and 65px Japanese columns force frequent character-level wrapping.

critique.good: Complete keys and headings make lookup easier. The initial viewport shows the key and English columns together, while the full table is substantially more compact than d1r0C. Most translations wrap into manageable blocks.
critique.problems: The email row is noticeably taller than the others, with Japanese broken into three short lines. Some word breaks remain. Comparing distant languages requires scrolling, and the key may leave the viewport while doing so.
critique.cause: The 145px Japanese column is tight for the long email message; the 125px English and Arabic columns also constrain longer phrases. The 227px key column preserves identifiers but consumes most of the initial viewport.

critique.good: Every entry stays on one line, making the full table orderly and easy to scan by language or compare across a row when viewed in its entirety. Keys and text remain intact.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts off several English phrases and shows no translation column. The long horizontal journey makes row-by-row comparison on a phone cumbersome, while the generous widths leave substantial empty space in shorter entries.
critique.cause: The 217px English column extends well beyond the space remaining beside the 227px key column. The 205px Chinese, 304px Japanese and 208px Arabic columns accommodate their longest entries on one line, producing an 1162px table.

critique.good: All five columns are visible at once, and the row boundaries remain clear.
critique.problems: Keys, words, headers and the Chinese shipping range split across lines. Narrow CJK columns create nearly vertical text, while tall, uneven rows make it hard to read across or scan a column.
critique.cause: The 130px key column cannot contain the identifiers; the 45–75px language columns leave too little text space for words and natural phrases.

critique.good: Intact keys and mostly natural line breaks make the table easy to scan. No cell exceeds two lines, and the initial viewport shows the key and English columns together.
critique.problems: Translations require substantial horizontal travel, and the first viewport gives no visible indication of the Chinese column. The long Japanese email message breaks within a term.
critique.cause: The 227px key and 132px English columns consume the initial viewport; the 180px Japanese column still requires the longest sentence to wrap.

critique.good: Keys remain intact, the initial viewport still shows the key and English together, and the table requires less horizontal travel than d1r1B.
critique.problems: The Japanese email message occupies three lines and splits a term; the shipping message also breaks awkwardly. The taller email row introduces extra blank space across the other columns.
critique.cause: The 145px Japanese column is too narrow for a more natural two-line treatment. The narrower Arabic column also adds wrapping in the search and shipping rows.

critique.good: All five columns are visible at once, and the key column preserves more of each identifier per line than d1r1A.
critique.problems: The header is unusually tall, Chinese and Japanese read in narrow vertical fragments, and English and Arabic words split repeatedly. The email row becomes extremely tall, making it difficult to follow translations across the row.
critique.cause: The 150px key column leaves only 38px for Chinese, 50px for Japanese, 49px for Arabic, and 72px for English.

critique.good: Keys stay intact, English is readable at first sight, and most translations wrap into manageable lines. The full table has a clear hierarchy and compact rows.
critique.problems: The Chinese email translation occupies three lines and makes that row taller than its neighbors. The initial viewport shows no translation columns, so comparison requires horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 105px Chinese column is too narrow for the email text in two lines. The 227px key and 132px English columns use the initial viewport.

critique.good: The table requires less horizontal travel than the other scrolling designs, and a portion of Chinese appears initially. Most language cells remain reasonably readable.
critique.problems: Several keys break within identifiers, including a single trailing letter in the first row. The Japanese email message takes three lines, and the narrow Chinese column also makes that row tall.
critique.cause: The 190px key column is narrower than the longest identifier plus padding; the 160px Japanese and 100px Chinese columns constrain the email row.

critique.good: All columns are visible, and its more balanced allocation reduces the extreme height seen in d1r2A. English fits on one line in the header.
critique.problems: Every key breaks, and several English and Arabic words split. Chinese and Japanese are still set in very narrow fragments; the shipping range also breaks in Chinese. The tall rows make cross-language comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 130px key column cannot contain the identifiers, while 75px for English and 45–61px would be needed just to begin accommodating larger semantic units in the other columns; the actual Chinese, Japanese, and Arabic widths are 45px, 55px, and 54px.

critique.good: This is the strongest scrolling render: keys remain intact, all cells fit within two lines, and the more generous Chinese column keeps the email row compact. The first viewport supports key and English lookup.
critique.problems: Translations are entirely beyond the initial viewport, and reaching Arabic requires substantial horizontal travel. Some phrases wrap even though the full table is already wide.
critique.cause: The 227px key and 132px English columns fill the first viewport; the remaining 125px, 180px, and 155px language columns extend the table to 820px.

critique.good: All five columns are visible without scrolling, and the English text mostly wraps at word boundaries.
critique.problems: Keys break repeatedly, three language headers wrap, and Chinese and Japanese run in narrow vertical stacks. The email and shipping rows become exceptionally tall, making cross-language comparison difficult.
critique.cause: The 105px key column cannot hold the identifiers; the 49px Chinese and 61px Japanese and Arabic columns leave too little room for natural reading.

critique.good: Keys and headers are intact, and the initial viewport shows the key and English columns together. Its relatively compact width reduces horizontal travel.
critique.problems: The Japanese email message takes three lines, making that row disproportionately tall. Some wording breaks inside words, and all translations start beyond the initial viewport.
critique.cause: The 145px Japanese column is too narrow for a more natural two-line email message; the 120px Arabic column also constrains word wrapping. The 227px key column consumes much of the viewport, though it preserves identifiers.

critique.good: The measured text has no breaks inside words, and the table is short and easy to scan when viewed in full. The language columns provide comfortable reading space.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through English wording, so even the source text requires scrolling. The generous overall width also increases travel between the key and Arabic.
critique.cause: The 227px key and 215px English columns together exceed the viewport; the 205px Chinese column contributes substantially to the 983px table width.

critique.good: More of each key is visible per line than in d1r3A, and all columns remain on screen.
critique.problems: Identifiers still break, while English words, Arabic words and the Chinese shipping range split. Three headers wrap, and narrow CJK columns create tall, fragmented rows.
critique.cause: Increasing the key column to 130px leaves only 75px for English and 45–55px for each translation column; those widths are insufficient for their content.

critique.good: Intact keys and a fully visible English column make the initial viewport useful for lookup. The full table has no cells taller than two lines, and Japanese and Arabic read more comfortably than in d1r3B.
critique.problems: One measured break remains inside a word. Chinese shipping text wraps, and translations remain outside the initial viewport; reading through to Arabic requires substantial horizontal travel.
critique.cause: The 125px Chinese column and 132px English column favor a compact first view, while the 180px Japanese and 155px Arabic columns add width to preserve more natural wrapping.

critique.good: All five columns are visible at once. The Chinese header remains on one line, and the English column supports some recognizable phrases.
critique.problems: Keys and English and Arabic words break internally; Japanese and Arabic headers also wrap. The invalid-email row becomes especially tall, disrupting scanning and comparison.
critique.cause: At 110 px, the key column cannot hold the identifiers. The 54–58 px translation columns are too narrow for continuous reading, especially the 58 px Japanese column.
